modern_osis:
Psalms — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

David wrote most of the Psalms, though some were plainly written by others and the authorship of some is uncertain.

All were written through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

No part of the Old Testament is cited or referred to more often in the New Testament.

Every Psalm either points directly to Christ—his person, character and offices—or can lead believers to think about him.

The Psalms give words to the hearts of believers in every condition: mourning over sin, longing for God or rejoicing in him; bearing affliction, struggling with temptation or celebrating the hope or experience of deliverance; contemplating God's perfections, thanking him for his mercy, meditating on his truths or delighting in his service.

They provide a divinely appointed measure of spiritual experience by which believers can examine themselves.

As true religion grows stronger within the heart, the Psalms become increasingly valuable.

Through the psalmists' words, the Spirit helps us pray.

When we become familiar with them, we find help approaching the throne of grace to confess sin, ask for mercy or give thanks.

Whatever holy affection fills the heart—desire, hope, sorrow or joy—we can find worthy language for it in this book.

Through the generations, the church has offered its prayers and praises to God using these inspired words.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe holiness and happiness of a godly man.1–3The sinfulness and misery of a wicked man, The ground and reason of both.4–6
The godly person and God's word (verses 1–3)

To meditate on God's word means to speak with ourselves about the great truths it contains, applying our minds closely and thinking about them steadily.

God's word should guide our actions and provide our comfort.

We should keep it continually in our minds both day and night.

No time is unsuitable for meditating upon it.

The ungodly person and final judgment (verses 4–6)

The ungodly differ from the righteous both in character and in condition.

Instead of delighting in God's law, they accept wicked advice, walk in sinful ways and finally settle into the position of those who mock what is holy.

They produce no good fruit.

The righteous resemble useful, fruitful trees.

But the ungodly resemble chaff blown away by wind—the worthless material a farmer wants removed from the threshing floor.

They have no spiritual value before God, however highly they regard themselves.

Every new temptation can blow them in a different direction.

Chaff may remain mixed with wheat for a time, but the One who holds the winnowing fan will completely cleanse his threshing floor.

Those who have made themselves like chaff through sin and folly will be found to be so when God's judgment comes like a storm and fire.

The final outcome of the ungodly is fixed if they remain in their sin.

Yet someone who recognizes guilt and misery may enter the company of the righteous through Jesus Christ, the living way.

In him that sinner becomes a new creation.

Desires, pleasures, hopes, fears, sorrows, friendships, occupations, thoughts, words and deeds are all changed.

Through divine grace, the person takes on a new life and character, as the soul is increasingly transformed into the Redeemer's image.

How different the characters and final outcomes of the righteous and ungodly are!
classic_reading:
[Ps.1.1-Ps.1.3]
Psalms
David was the penman of most of the psalms, but some evidently were composed by other writers, and the writers of some are doubtful. But all were written by the inspiration of the Holy Ghost; and no part of the Old Testament is more frequently quoted or referred to in the New. Every psalm either points directly to Christ, in his person, his character, and offices; or may lead the believer's thoughts to Him. And the psalms are the language of the believer's heart, whether mourning for sin, thirsting after God, or rejoicing in Him. Whether burdened with affliction, struggling with temptation, or triumphing in the hope or enjoyment of deliverance; whether admiring the Divine perfections, thanking God for his mercies, mediating on his truths, or delighting in his service; they form a Divinely appointed standard of experience, by which we may judge ourselves. Their value, in this view, is very great, and the use of them will increase with the growth of the power of true religion in the heart. By the psalmist's expressions, the Spirit helps us to pray. If we make the psalms familiar to us, whatever we have to ask at the throne of grace, by way of confession, petition, or thanksgiving, we may be assisted from thence. Whatever devout affection is working in us, holy desire or hope, sorrow or joy, we may here find words to clothe it; sound speech which cannot be condemned. In the language of this Divine book, the prayers and praises of the church have been offered up to the throne of grace from age to age.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The holiness and happiness of a godly man. | (1-3) |
The sinfulness and misery of a wicked man, The ground and reason of both. | (4-6) |
Verses 1-3
To meditate in God's word, is to discourse with ourselves concerning the great things contained in it, with close application of mind and fixedness of thought. We must have constant regard to the word of God, as the rule of our actions, and the spring of our comforts; and have it in our thoughts night and day. For this purpose no time is amiss.
[Ps.1.4-Ps.1.6]
Verses 4-6
The ungodly are the reverse of the righteous, both in character and condition. The ungodly are not so, ver. 4; they are led by the counsel of the wicked, in the way of sinners, to the seat of the scornful; they have no delight in the law of God; they bring forth no fruit but what is evil. The righteous are like useful, fruitful trees: the ungodly are like the chaff which the wind drives away: the dust which the owner of the floor desires to have driven away, as not being of any use. They are of no worth in God's account, how highly soever they may value themselves. They are easily driven to and fro by every wind of temptation. The chaff may be, for a while, among the wheat, but He is coming, whose fan is in his hand, and who will thoroughly purge his floor. Those that, by their own sin and folly, make themselves as chaff, will be found so before the whirlwind and fire of Divine wrath. The doom of the ungodly is fixed, but whenever the sinner becomes sensible of this guilt and misery, he may be admitted into the company of the righteous by Christ the living way, and become in Christ a new creature. He has new desires, new pleasures, hopes, fears, sorrows, companions, and employments. His thoughts, words, and actions are changed. He enters on a new state, and bears a new character. Behold, all things are become new by Divine grace, which changes his soul into the image of the Redeemer. How different the character and end of the ungodly!

The enemies of Christ's kingdom (verses 1–6)

The Psalm describes those who oppose Christ.

The present world is under Satan's rule, and people without saving grace, of every social position, party and character, can be stirred by him against God's cause.

Earthly rulers have often been particularly active in this opposition.

Christian truth and the commands of Christ expose the ambitions and selfish desires of worldly power.

His opponents want to cast off the restraints of conscience and the commands of God, treating them as chains to be broken.

Yet they can give no good reason for rejecting a government so righteous and holy that, if everyone received it, it would make earthly life resemble heaven.

Their resistance cannot succeed against so powerful a kingdom.

Jesus Christ possesses all authority in heaven and on earth.

He is Head over everything for the church, whatever plans his enemies make.

His throne is established within his church, in the hearts of believers.

The Father's promise to the Son (verses 7–9)

The Messiah's kingdom rests upon the eternal decree of God the Father.

Jesus himself referred to that decree and conducted his mission accordingly.

God declared to him, “You are my Son.”

Each of us should answer, “You are my Lord and Sovereign.”

When the Son asks for the nations as his inheritance, he seeks their happiness in him.

He intercedes for them continually.

He lives forever to do this and can save completely everyone who comes to God through him.

Multitudes among the nations will become his willing and loyal subjects.

Christians belong to Jesus Christ.

They bring him honor and praise.

The Father gives them to the Son by working through the Spirit and grace so that they gladly submit to Jesus.

The call to trust and serve Christ (verses 10–12)

Whatever we enjoy in this world, we should rejoice with reverence, because every earthly possession and circumstance is uncertain.

Welcoming Jesus Christ and submitting to him is both our duty and our greatest good.

Let him become precious to us.

Love him sincerely and deeply, as the woman who had been forgiven much showed her love by kissing his feet (Luke 7:38).

Greet the Son with a kiss of loyalty.

Accept his rule, submit to his laws, entrust your circumstances to his Providence and give yourselves entirely to his cause.

Unbelief rejects the only remedy for sin.

It will bring destruction to those who persist in it.

They will perish in their sinful path, in their empty hopes and in the loss of the true way to happiness.

Christ is the way to God.

People may suppose they are walking the right path, but if they reject Christ they will lose it.

Blessed are those who have made Christ their Refuge through faith.

They will be safe even on the day of divine wrath.
classic_reading:
[Ps.2.1-Ps.2.6]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Threatenings against the enemies of Christ's kingdom. | (1-6) |
Promise to Christ as the Head of this kingdom. | (7-9) |
Counsel to all, to espouse its interests. | (10-12) |
Verses 1-6
We are here told who would appear as adversaries to Christ. As this world is the kingdom of Satan, unconverted men, of every rank, party, and character, are stirred up by him to oppose the cause of God. But the rulers of the earth generally have been most active. The truths and precepts of Christianity are against ambitious projects and worldly lusts. We are told what they aim at in this opposition. They would break asunder the bands of conscience, and the cords of God's commandments; they will not receive, but cast them away as far as they can. These enemies can show no good cause for opposing so just and holy a government, which, if received by all, would bring a heaven upon earth. They can hope for no success in so opposing so powerful a kingdom. The Lord Jesus has all power both in heaven and in earth, and is Head over all things to the church, notwithstanding the restless endeavours of his enemies. Christ's throne is set up in his church, that is, in the hearts of all believers.
[Ps.2.7-Ps.2.9]
Verses 7-9
The kingdom of the Messiah is founded upon an eternal decree of God the Father. This our Lord Jesus often referred to, as what he governed himself by. God hath said unto him, Thou art my Son, and it becomes each of us to say to him, Thou art my Lord, my Sovereign'. The Son, in asking the heathen for his inheritance, desires their happiness in him; so that he pleads for them, ever lives to do so, and is able to save to the uttermost, and he shall have multitudes of willing, loyal subjects, among them. Christians are the possession of the Lord Jesus; they are to him for a name and a praise. God the Father gives them to him, when, by his Spirit and grace, he works upon them to submit to the Lord Jesus.
[Ps.2.10-Ps.2.12]
Verses 10-12
Whatever we rejoice in, in this world, it must always be with trembling, because of the uncertainty of all things in it. To welcome Jesus Christ, and to submit to him, is our wisdom and interest. Let him be very dear and precious; love him above all, love him in sincerity, love him much, as she did, to whom much was forgiven, and, in token of it, kissed his feet, [Luke.7.38] Lu 7:38. And with a kiss of loyalty take this yoke upon you, and give up yourselves to be governed by his laws, disposed of by his providence, and entirely devoted to his cause. Unbelief is a sin against the remedy. It will be utter destruction to yourselves; lest ye perish in the way of your sins, and from the way of your vain hopes; lest your way perish, lest you prove to have missed the way of happiness. Christ is the way; take heed lest ye be cut off from Him as your way to God. They thought themselves in the way; but neglecting Christ, they perish from it. Blessed will those be in the day of wrath, who, by trusting in Christ, have made him their Refuge.

David trusts God while enemies surround him (verses 1–3)

The more an active believer is driven away from God by painful Providence or the accusations of enemies, the more firmly that person clings to him.

A child of God is alarmed even by the thought of despairing of divine help.

David knew that God provided his people with three blessings.

First, safety: the Lord was his shield, protecting him.

Second, honor: everyone whom God receives as his own possesses genuine dignity.

Third, joy and deliverance: even in the worst times, believers may lift their heads with gladness, knowing that everything will work for their good.

They recognize that God gives them both reasons to rejoice and hearts capable of rejoicing.

Prayer, rest and victory through God (verses 4–8)

Distress and sorrow bring good when they lead us to pray earnestly.

David had repeatedly found God ready to answer.

Nothing can sever the connection between God's favor toward us and the faith he produces within us.

David had lived safely under God's protection.

Even the ordinary mercy of sleeping each night deserves our thanks every morning.

Many people cannot sleep because of pain, anxiety or frightening events.

But David's words especially describe his inner calm amid danger.

Through grace and the comforts of the Holy Spirit, the Lord gave him peace.

A mind resting firmly upon God is a great mercy in trouble.

Consider the Son of David lying down to rest on the cross, that bed of sorrows, and entrusting his Spirit to the Father's hands with confidence in a joyful resurrection.

Christian, let faith teach you how to sleep and how to die.

Sleep is a brief kind of death, and death is a longer sleep.

The same God watches over you on your bed and in your grave.

David's faith became triumphant.

He began by describing his enemies' strength and cruelty.

He finished by rejoicing in God's power and grace, recognizing that more were on his side than against him.

Salvation belongs to the Lord.

No danger exceeds his power to save.

Those who know the Lord as their God can be sure of salvation, for he is the God of salvation.
classic_reading:
[Ps.3.1-Ps.3.3]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
David complains to God of his enemies, and confides in God. | (1-3) |
He triumphs over his fears, and gives God the glory, and takes to himself the comfort. | (4-8) |
Verses 1-3
An active believer, the more he is beaten off from God, either by the rebukes of providence, or the reproaches of enemies, the faster hold he will take, and the closer will he cleave to him. A child of God startles at the very thought of despairing of help in God. See what God is to his people, what he will be, what they have found him, what David found in him. 1. Safety; a shield for me; which denotes the advantage of that protection. 2. Honour; those whom God owns for his, have true honour put upon them. 3. Joy and deliverance. If, in the worst of times, God's people can lift up their heads with joy, knowing that all shall work for good to them, they will own God as giving them both cause and hearts to rejoice.
[Ps.3.4-Ps.3.8]
Verses 4-8
Care and grief do us good, when they engage us to pray to God, as in earnest. David had always found God ready to answer his prayers. Nothing can fix a gulf between the communications of God's grace towards us, and the working of his grace in us; between his favour and our faith. He had always been very safe under the Divine protection. This is applicable to the common mercies of every night, for which we ought to give thanks every morning. Many lie down, and cannot sleep, through pain of body, or anguish of mind, or the continual alarms of fear in the night. But it seems here rather to be meant of the calmness of David's spirit, in the midst of his dangers. The Lord, by his grace and the consolations of his Spirit, made him easy. It is a great mercy, when we are in trouble, to have our minds stayed upon God. Behold the Son of David composing himself to his rest upon the cross, that bed of sorrows; commending his Spirit into the Father's hands in full confidence of a joyful resurrection. Behold this, O Christian: let faith teach thee how to sleep, and how to die; while it assures thee that as sleep is a short death, so death is only a longer sleep; the same God watches over thee, in thy bed and in thy grave. David's faith became triumphant. He began the psalm with complaints of the strength and malice of his enemies; but concludes with rejoicing in the power and grace of his God, and now sees more with him than against him. Salvation belongeth unto the Lord; he has power to save, be the danger ever so great. All that have the Lord for their God, are sure of salvation; for he who is their God, is the God of Salvation.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe children of men proved, and the happiness of godly people.1–5God's favour is happiness.6–8
Reverence, self-examination and trust (verses 1–5)

Our strongest plea in prayer is to ask God to hear us for his mercy's sake.

People who refuse to ask for forgiveness, the righteousness that justifies and eternal life will perish because they have rejected blessings they desperately need.

It is a dreadful choice.

The psalmist warns against sin.

Keep a holy reverence for God's greatness and glory.

There is much we ought to say to our own hearts.

Do not leave it unsaid.

Examine your heart through serious reflection.

Fix your thoughts on what is good and hold to it.

Before going to sleep, review the day's conduct and ask especially what you did wrong, so that you can repent.

When you wake at night, meditate on God and what leads to peace with him.

During illness, give particular attention to examining your ways.

Be still.

When you question your conscience, remain serious and quiet long enough to hear its answer.

Do not rush to excuse sin.

All confidence must rest in God alone.

Therefore, after speaking of sacrifices offered in righteousness, the psalmist commands us to trust in the Lord.

The happiness of God's favor (verses 6–8)

Worldly people ask for good things, but not usually the greatest good.

They want outward, immediate and partial benefits: good food and drink, a successful business, comfortable possessions and wealth.

But how much are these worth?

Most people will accept almost any benefit.

Someone whose heart is ruled by grace cannot be satisfied with these things alone.

Such a person prays: Lord, let us know your favor. Let us be sure of your loving kindness. That is enough.

Many people search for happiness.

David had found it.

When God gives grace to the heart, he also gives gladness to the heart.

Comforted in this way, David could pity prosperous sinners without envying or fearing them.

He committed his concerns to God and became willing to accept God's wise will.

But salvation is in Jesus Christ alone.

Those who reject him as Mediator and insult him through his disciples are in grave danger.

May they stand in awe, turn from sin and stop resisting the only remedy.

[Ps.4.1-Ps.4.5]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The children of men proved, and the happiness of godly people. | (1-5) |
God's favour is happiness. | (6-8) |
Verses 1-5
Hear me for thy mercy-sake, is our best plea. He who will not ask such blessings as pardon, and justifying righteousness, and eternal life, must perish for the want of them. Alas! that so many should make so fearful a choice. The psalmist warns against sin. Keep up holy reverence of the glory and majesty of God. You have a great deal to say to your hearts, they may be spoken with, let it not be unsaid. Examine them by serious self-reflection; let your thoughts fasten upon that which is good, and keep close to it. Consider your ways, and before you turn to sleep at night, examine your consciences with respect to what you have done in the day; particularly what you have done amiss, that you may repent of it. when you awake in the night, meditate upon God, and the things that belong to your peace. Upon a sick-bed, particularly, we should consider our ways. Be still. when you have asked conscience a question, be serious, be silent, wait for an answer. Open not the mouth to excuse sin. All confidence must be pan answer. Open not the mouth to excuse sin. All confidence only: therefore, after commanding the sacrifices of righteousness, the psalmist says, Put your trust in the Lord.
[Ps.4.6-Ps.4.8]
Verses 6-8
Wordly people inquire for good, not for the chief good; all they want is outward good, present good, partial good, good meat, good drink, a good trade, and a good estate; but what are all these worth? Any good will serve the turn of most men, but a gracious soul will not be put off so. Lord, let us have thy favour, and let us know that we have it, we desire no more; let us be satisfied of thy loving-kindness, and will be satisfied with it. Many inquire after happiness, but David had found it. When God puts grace in the heart, he puts gladness in the heart. Thus comforted, he pitied, but neither envied nor feared the most prosperous sinner. He commits all his affairs to God, and is prepared to welcome his holy will. But salvation is in Christ alone; where will those appear who despise him as their Mediator, and revile him in his disciples? May they stand in awe, and no longer sin against the only remedy.

The God who hears prayer (verses 1–6)

God hears prayer.

He has always done so, and he remains as ready to receive prayer as ever.

One of our strongest reasons for confidence in prayer is that we approach him as our King and our God.

David prayed to the God who hates sin.

Sin is folly.

Those who persist in it are fools of their own making.

People who are determined to be wicked hate God and rightly face his judgment.

If they continue in that condition, their misery and destruction will be everlasting.

We should learn to value truthfulness and sincerity in every part of life.

Liars and murderers resemble the devil and show whose ways they follow.

The Lord abhors such wrongdoing.

David's enemies displayed these characteristics.

People who behave in the same way still oppose Christ and his church.

God guides, protects and brings joy (verses 7–12)

David regularly prayed on his own.

Yet he was also faithful in attending public worship.

God's mercy must always be the foundation of our hope and joy in everything involving him.

Our prayers should reach beyond ourselves to other believers.

Grace be with everyone who sincerely loves Jesus Christ.

Every blessing comes through Jesus Christ, the Righteous One, just as God's favor was previously shown to Israel through David, whom he protected and established upon the throne.

Christ is the righteous Savior, Israel's King and the source of blessing for every believer.

His favor is the defense and protection of his church.

[Ps.5.1-Ps.5.6]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
God will certainly hear prayer: David gives to God the glory, and takes to himself the comfort. | (1-6) |
He prayed for himself, that God would guide him, and for all the Lord's people, that God would give them joy, and keep them safe. | (7-12) |
Verses 1-6
God is a prayer-hearing God. Such he has always been, and he is still as ready to hear prayer as ever. The most encouraging principle of prayer, and the most powerful plea in prayer, is, to look upon him as our King and our God. David also prays to a sin-hating God. sin is folly, and sinners are the greatest of all fools; fools of their own making. Wicked people hate God; justly are they hated of him, and this will be their endless misery and ruin. Let us learn the importance of truth and sincerity, in all the affairs of life. Liars and murderers resemble the devil, and are his children, therefore it may well be expected that God should abhor them. These were the characters of David's enemies; and such as these are still the enemies of Christ and his people.
[Ps.5.7-Ps.5.12]
Verses 7-12
David prayed often alone, yet was very constant in attendance on public worship. The mercy of God should ever be the foundation both of our hope and of our joy, in every thing wherein we have to do with him. Let us learn to pray, not for ourselves only, but for others; grace be with all that love Christ in sincerity. The Divine blessing comes down upon us through Jesus Christ, the righteous or just One, as of old it did upon Israel through David, whom God protected, and placed upon the throne. Thou, O Christ, art the righteous Saviour, thou art the King of Israel, thou art the Fountain of blessing to all believers; thy favour is the defence and protection of thy church.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe psalmist deprecates God's wrath, and begs for the return of his favour.1–7He assures himself of an answer of peace.8–10
A humbled heart seeks divine favor (verses 1–7)

These words express a truly humbled heart, a broken and contrite spirit enduring great suffering.

The affliction was allowed to awaken the psalmist's conscience and help put sinful desires to death.

Illness reminded him of his sins, and he feared that it showed God's displeasure.

Bodily suffering can be endured when the soul enjoys God's consolation.

In his own suffering, Christ's deepest complaint concerned the anguish of his soul and the apparent withdrawal of his Father's favor.

Every part of Scripture declares that salvation belongs to the Lord alone.

Human beings are sinners, whose condition can be remedied only by mercy.

That mercy shines especially brightly when God restores people who have wandered from him.

We may rightly pray that, if it is God's will and he has further work for us or our loved ones to do on earth, he will preserve our lives for continued service.

For the saints, departing to be with Christ is the greater happiness.

Yet remaining alive may be more useful for the church.

Confidence that God will answer (verses 8–10)

What a remarkable change in the psalmist's words!

After laying his request before God, he became confident that sorrow would turn into joy.

Through grace working within his heart, he knew his prayer had been accepted and trusted that an answer would come in due time.

Our prayers are acceptable because they rise to God through the hands of Christ our Mediator.

The words describe prayer to God as the righteous Judge and the God of the believer's righteousness, who will defend the right and put wrongs right.

Through Christ's blood and righteousness, a believer can approach a righteous God to ask for forgiveness and cleansing.

God is both just and faithful to grant these blessings.

The psalmist's words regarding his enemies may be either a prayer for their conversion or a prediction of their downfall.
classic_reading:
[Ps.6.1-Ps.6.7]
Chapter 6
Chapter Outline
The psalmist deprecates God's wrath, and begs for the return of his favour. | (1-7) |
He assures himself of an answer of peace. | (8-10) |
Verses 1-7
These verses speak the language of a heart truly humbled, of a broken and contrite spirit under great afflictions, sent to awaken conscience and mortify corruption. Sickness brought sin to his remembrance, and he looked upon it as a token of God's displeasure against him. The affliction of his body will be tolerable, if he has comfort in his soul. Christ's sorest complaint, in his sufferings, was of the trouble of his soul, and the want of his Father's smiles. Every page of Scripture proclaims the fact, that salvation is only of the Lord. Man is a sinner, his case can only be reached by mercy; and never is mercy more illustrious than in restoring backsliders. With good reason we may pray, that if it be the will of God, and he has any further work for us or our friends to do in this world, he will yet spare us or them to serve him. To depart and be with Christ is happiest for the saints; but for them to abide in the flesh is more profitable for the church.
[Ps.6.8-Ps.6.10]
Verses 8-10
What a sudden change is here! Having made his request known to God, the psalmist is confident that his sorrow will be turned into joy. By the workings of God's grace upon his heart, he knew his prayer was accepted, and did not doubt but it would, in due time, be answered. His prayers will be accepted, coming up out of the hands of Christ the Mediator. The word signifies prayer made to God, the righteous Judge, as the God of his righteousness, who would plead his cause, and right his wrongs. A believer, through the blood and righteousness of Christ, can go to God as a righteous God, and plead with him for pardon and cleansing, who is just and faithful to grant both. He prays for the conversion of his enemies, or foretells their ruin.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe psalmist prays to God to plead his cause, and judge for him.1–9He expresses confidence in God, and will give him the glory of his deliverance.10–17
David appeals to the Judge of hearts (verses 1–9)

David fled to God for help and protection.

Yet Jesus Christ alone could call heaven to witness that he was completely upright in every respect.

All his works were righteous.

The prince of this world could find nothing in him that deserved accusation.

Nevertheless, for our sake Christ accepted being treated as guilty and suffered every evil.

He remained innocent and triumphed over them all.

David's appeal was directed to the righteous God who examines hearts and the deepest desires.

God knows the hidden sins of wicked people and how to bring their wrongdoing to an end.

He also knows the secret sincerity of those who live uprightly and can establish their cause.

Anyone who has first made peace with God concerning personal sins through the sacrifice of the Mediator, according to God's mercy and grace, may then appeal to divine justice when falsely accused by enemies.

The righteous God saves and warns (verses 10–17)

David trusted that God would be a powerful Savior.

The threatened destruction of a sinner may be avoided through repentance and conversion.

The warning is therefore an act of mercy.

God gives people time to repent and escape the judgment they otherwise face.

He is patient and slow to punish, not delighting in the destruction of sinners.

In verses 14–16, sinners are pictured exerting great effort in destroying their own souls.

If those same efforts were turned toward repentance and obedience, they could lead toward salvation.

In this sense, the description applies to everyone who continues in sin.

Throughout our trials we must look to the Savior.

Blessed Lord, grant that we may follow your spotless example as you go before your church in suffering.

When persecution and trouble mark our smaller path, may looking to Jesus strengthen our minds and comfort our hearts.
classic_reading:
[Ps.7.1-Ps.7.9]
Chapter 7
Chapter Outline
The psalmist prays to God to plead his cause, and judge for him. | (1-9) |
He expresses confidence in God, and will give him the glory of his deliverance. | (10-17) |
Verses 1-9
David flees to God for succour. But Christ alone could call on Heaven to attest his uprightness in all things. All His works were wrought in righteousness; and the prince of this world found nothing whereof justly to accuse him. Yet for our sakes, submitting to be charged as guilty, he suffered all evils, but, being innocent, he triumphed over them all. The plea is, "For the righteous God trieth the hearts and the reins." He knows the secret wickedness of the wicked, and how to bring it to an end; he is witness to the secret sincerity of the just, and has ways of establishing it. When a man has made peace with God about all his sins, upon the terms of grace and mercy, through the sacrifice of the Mediator, he may, in comparison with his enemies, appeal to God's justice to decide.
[Ps.7.10-Ps.7.17]
Verses 10-17
David is confident that he shall find God his powerful Saviour. The destruction of sinners may be prevented by their conversion; for it is threatened, If he turn not from his evil way, let him expect it will be his ruin. But amidst the threatenings of wrath, we have a gracious offer of mercy. God gives sinners warning of their danger, and space to repent, and prevent it. He is slow to punish, and long-suffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish. The sinner is described, ver. #(14-16), as taking more pains to ruin his soul than, if directed aright, would save it. This is true, in a sense, of all sinners. Let us look to the Saviour under all our trials. Blessed Lord, give us grace to look to thee in the path of tribulation, going before thy church and people, and marking the way by thine own spotless example. Under all the persecutions which in our lesser trials mark our way, let the looking to Jesus animate our minds and comfort our hearts.

God's name is glorious (verses 1 and 2)

The psalmist wanted to give God the glory his name deserves.

How brightly that glory shines even in our earthly world!

God is our Lord because he created us, protects us and cares for us specially.

The birth, earthly life, preaching, miracles, suffering, death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ have become known throughout the world.

No other name is so widely recognized and no influence so generally felt as the Savior's.

But divine glory shines even more brilliantly in heaven.

Here on earth we hear God's excellent name and praise it.

The angels and blessed spirits see his glory and praise him for it.

Nevertheless, God is exalted beyond even their worship and thanksgiving.

Sometimes divine grace is seen wonderfully in little children.

At other times God accomplishes great things within his church through weak and unlikely people, so that everyone can recognize that the power came from him, not them.

Through such actions he silences his enemies.

Humanity's dignity under God and Christ (verses 3–9)

Considering the heavens should lead us to turn our desires toward heavenly things.

What are human beings—so small—that God should honor them?

What are human beings—so sinful—that he should show them favor?

Humanity has been given authority over lesser creatures, subject to God.

This passage also points specifically to Jesus Christ.

In Hebrews 2:6–8, the apostle uses these words to demonstrate Christ's supreme authority.

Jesus is the Man and Son of Man who has received dominion over the works of God's hands.

The greatest honor ever given to human nature, and the greatest mercy ever shown to our race, are displayed in Christ.

The psalmist therefore had every reason to finish as he began:

Lord, how excellent is your name in all the earth!

The earth has been honored by the Redeemer's presence and continues to receive the light of his gospel and the governance of his wisdom and power.

How could our words be sufficient to praise the One who has every right to our obedience as Redeemer?

Verses 1-2
The psalmist seeks to give unto God the glory due to his name. How bright this glory shines even in this lower world! He is ours, for he made us, protects us, and takes special care of us. The birth, life, preaching, miracles, suffering, death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus are known through the world. No name is so universal, no power and influence so generally felt, as those of the Saviour of mankind. But how much brighter it shines in the upper world! We, on this earth, only hear God's excellent name, and praise that; the angels and blessed spirits above, see his glory, and praise that; yet he is exalted far above even their blessing and praise. Sometimes the grace of God appears wonderfully in young children. Sometimes the power of God brings to pass great things in his church, by very weak and unlikely instruments, that the excellency of the power might the more evidently appear to be of God, and not of man. This he does, because of his enemies, that he may put them to silence.
[Ps.8.3-Ps.8.9]
Verses 3-9
We are to consider the heavens, that man thus may be directed to set his affections on things above. What is man, so mean a creature, that he should be thus honoured! so sinful a creature, that he should be thus favoured! Man has sovereign dominion over the inferior creatures, under God, and is appointed their lord. This refers to Christ. In [Heb.2.6-Heb.2.8] He 2:6-8, the apostle, to prove the sovereign dominion of Christ, shows he is that Man, that Son of man, here spoken of, whom God has made to have dominion over the works of his hands. With good reason does the psalmist conclude as he began, Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth, which has been honoured with the presence of the Redeemer, and is still enlightened by his gospel, and governed by his wisdom and power! What words can reach his praises, who has a right to our obedience as our Redeemer?

David thanks God for protecting his people (verses 1–10)

For our praise to be acceptable to God, we must offer it sincerely with our whole hearts.

When thanking him for a particular mercy, remember the earlier mercies already received.

Our greatest joy must be in the Giver, not merely the gift.

The victories of the Redeemer should be celebrated as the victories of all the redeemed.

The strongest of God's enemies are powerless before his almighty strength.

We can be confident that the Lord's judgments are true and free of all injustice.

His people may flee to him through faith as their Refuge.

They can depend upon his power and promises for safety, so that no lasting harm comes upon them.

Those who recognize God as faithful and truthful will rejoice in his promises and rest upon them.

Those who know him as their everlasting Father will entrust their souls to him as their greatest concern.

They will trust him continually, persevering in faithful service throughout life.

Who would refuse to seek the One who has never abandoned those who seek him?

Reasons to call others to praise (verses 11–20)

People who truly believe God deserves praise do not want merely to praise him more faithfully themselves.

They also want others to join them.

The day is coming when God will show that he has not forgotten the cries of humble people—their prayers or the testimony of their blood.

No suffering can bring us so low, or so close to death, that God cannot raise us up.

If he has already rescued us from spiritual and eternal death, we can confidently look to him for help in every distress.

God's Providence often brings wicked people to ruin through the very plans they made to destroy others.

The drunkard destroys his health.

The spendthrift impoverishes himself.

The quarrelsome person brings trouble upon his own life.

These examples show how sin contains the seeds of its punishment.

The ultimate destruction of those who continue in sin comes through their own choices.

Sin originally entered human life through the wicked one.

Those who stubbornly remain under his dominion face his dreadful end.

The true condition of nations and individuals can be measured by a simple question:

Do their actions show that they remember God, or that they have forgotten him?

David urged God's people to wait patiently for deliverance, even when it appears long delayed.

God will prove that he has never forgotten them.

How strange that human beings—creatures made of dust and destined for dust—often need severe suffering before they recognize who they are!

Chapter Outline
David praises God for protecting his people. | (1-10) |
And for cause to praise him. | (11-20) |
Verses 1-10
If we would praise God acceptably, we must praise him in sincerity, with our whole heart. When we give thanks for some one particular mercy, we should remember former mercies. Our joy must not be in the gift, so much as in the Giver. The triumphs of the Redeemer ought to be the triumphs of the redeemed. The almighty power of God is that which the strongest and stoutest of his enemies are no way able to stand before. We are sure that the judgment of God is according to truth, and that with him there is no unrighteousness. His people may, by faith, flee to him as their Refuge, and may depend on his power and promise for their safety, so that no real hurt shall be done to them. Those who know him to be a God of truth and faithfulness, will rejoice in his word of promise, and rest upon that. Those who know him to be an everlasting Father, will trust him with their souls as their main care, and trust in him at all times, even to the end; and by constant care seek to approve themselves to him in the whole course of their lives. Who is there that would not seek him, who never hath forsaken those that seek Him?
[Ps.9.11-Ps.9.20]
Verses 11-20
Those who believe that God is greatly to be praised, not only desire to praise him better themselves, but desire that others may join with them. There is a day coming, when it will appear that he has not forgotten the cry of the humble; neither the cry of their blood, or the cry of their prayers. We are never brought so low, so near to death, but God can raise us up. If he has saved us from spiritual and eternal death, we may thence hope, that in all our distresses he will be a very present help to us. The overruling providence of God frequently so orders it, that persecutors and oppressors are brought to ruin by the projects they formed to destroy the people of God. Drunkards kill themselves; prodigals beggar themselves; the contentious bring mischief upon themselves: thus men's sins may be read in their punishment, and it becomes plain to all, that the destruction of sinners is of themselves. All wickedness came originally with the wicked one from hell; and those who continue in sin, must go to that place of torment. The true state, both of nations and of individuals, may be correctly estimated by this one rule, whether in their doings they remember or forget God. David encourages the people of God to wait for his salvation, though it should be long deferred. God will make it appear that he never did forget them: it is not possible he should. Strange that man, dust in his and about him, should yet need some sharp affliction, some severe visitation from God, to bring him to the knowledge of himself, and make him feel who and what he is.

The psalmist laments the wicked (verses 1–11)

When God seems to withdraw his presence, his people find it deeply painful, especially in trouble.

Often it is our unbelief that keeps us distant from God, even as we complain that he is distant from us.

Angry words against wicked people often accomplish more harm than good.

If we must speak of their sins, bring the matter before God in prayer.

He can transform them.

The sinner proudly celebrates worldly strength and success.

Wicked people do not seek God or call upon him.

To live without prayer is to live without God.

They think about countless projects, schemes and possessions, yet give no thought to God in any of them.

They do not submit to his will or seek his glory.

The cause is pride.

They imagine genuine religion is beneath them.

People would not so readily disregard justice and kindness toward other humans unless they had first rejected reverence for God.

A prayer for the oppressed and tempted (verses 12–18)

The psalmist was amazed both at the bold wickedness of human beings and at God's patience in allowing it to continue.

God prepares hearts for prayer.

He awakens holy desires, strengthens faith, directs attention and raises affections toward himself.

Then he graciously accepts the prayer.

Preparing the heart is itself God's work, so we should ask him to prepare our hearts.

Poor, afflicted, persecuted or tempted believers should remember that Satan is the prince of this present world and the father of the ungodly.

We cannot expect justice or mercy from people of the same spirit as those who crucified the Lord of glory.

But Jesus, who once suffered, now rules as King over all the earth.

His reign will never end.

Entrust yourselves to him, humbly relying on his mercy.

He will rescue his followers from every temptation, break the power of oppressors and soon crush Satan beneath their feet.

In this present life believers already taste something of the promised deliverance.

But only in heaven will sin and temptation finally be excluded altogether.

Chapter Outline

He prays to God to appear for the relief of his people. | (12-18) |
Verses 1-11
God's withdrawings are very grievous to his people, especially in times of trouble. We stand afar off from God by our unbelief, and then complain that God stands afar off from us. Passionate words against bad men do more hurt than good; if we speak of their badness, let it be to the Lord in prayer; he can make them better. The sinner proudly glories in his power and success. Wicked people will not seek after God, that is, will not call upon him. They live without prayer, and that is living without God. They have many thoughts, many objects and devices, but think not of the Lord in any of them; they have no submission to his will, nor aim for his glory. The cause of this is pride. Men think it below them to be religious. They could not break all the laws of justice and goodness toward man, if they had not first shaken off all sense of religion.
[Ps.10.12-Ps.10.18]
Verses 12-18
The psalmist speaks with astonishment, at the wickedness of the wicked, and at the patience and forbearance of God. God prepares the heart for prayer, by kindling holy desires, and strengthening our most holy faith, fixing the thoughts, and raising the affections, and then he graciously accepts the prayer. The preparation of the heart is from the Lord, and we must seek unto him for it. Let the poor, afflicted, persecuted, or tempted believer recollect, that Satan is the prince of this world, and that he is the father of all the ungodly. The children of God cannot expect kindness, truth, or justice from such persons as crucified the Lord of glory. But this once suffering Jesus, now reigns as King over all the earth, and of his dominion there shall be no end. Let us commit ourselves unto him, humbly trusting in his mercy. He will rescue the believer from every temptation, and break the arm of every wicked oppressor, and bruise Satan under our feet shortly. But in heaven alone will all sin and temptation be shut out, though in this life the believer has a foretaste of deliverance.
